top_articles.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
top_articles.title_original: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
top_articles.summary: Redesigning source control at Anthropic Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart ( code here ) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026: This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity. "Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. ( Update : Anthropic credit Google's Piper and Meta's Sapling as "prior art" - it looks like the core concept of "derived data" was heavily inspired by Mononoke , the server component of Sapling.) They had some pretty extreme requirements: The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day. The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months. When asked on Hacker News about the lack of offline support, Scion engineer Nick G replied : Since Claude is by far the heaviest user of Scion and is necessarily online, this just wasn't important to do. As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). This note from the article reflected my own experience with that: Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns. Via Hacker News Tags: git , migrations , version-control , ai , generative-ai , llms , anthropic , agentic-engineering

top_articles.title_original: LaTeX renderer
top_articles.summary: Tool: LaTeX renderer Inspired by Paul Ford and Aboard Foundary's new web app Tiny Little Office , which provides a suite of web app content editors (a Word Processor, Outliner, Presentation Builder, Spreadsheet, Calculator, Drawing Tool, Diagram Maker, Animator, Calendar, and Trip Planner). Tiny Little Office's signature trick is to store all of the document data in the #fragment section of the URL, so every document created using it becomes a bookmarkable and shareable link. It also has an llms.txt file telling agents how to construct URLs that will render as documents. Claude used that file to generate this link to a deck that explains how the URL format works: Tiny Little Office inspired me to have Claude Code (Opus 5.5 Extra) build a similar tool that works with LaTeX. Here's the sequence of prompts I used: I want a tool where you can link to it with a fragment hash #code-here and it treats that code as LaTeX and renders it really effectively. It should also support a prefix which means the latex is compressed with a custom compression dictionary optimized for latex. Use the best available latex render library from a CDN (consider WebAssembly too). If loaded without a fragment hash show an editor you can paste latex into and then toggle to a "rendered" view. That rendered view should be bookmarkable. The #fragment view should let you switch to edit source too. Since it was working in my tools repo I told it to take inspiration from the <iframe sandbox="..."> mechanism used by my existing SVG in Markdown tool as protection against XSS risks: Safe from XSS? We could run in an iframe sandbox like we do on the SVG markdown render project I had it copy the Gist/URL loading feature from that tool as well: We should have an option to load latex from a URL (or gist) similar to the markdown SVG tool Here's an example link . The tool uses Pako 2.1.0 , MathJax 4.1.3 , faster-latex 0.3.1 , and DOMPurify 3.4.16 . Tags: latex , paul-ford , tools , urls , ai , generative-ai , llms

top_articles.title: Who Verifies the Tools? How Warped Formatters Mislead Agents and Their Verifiers
top_articles.title_original: Who Verifies the Tools? How Warped Formatters Mislead Agents and Their Verifiers
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.32110v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agents and verifiers often rely on the text a tool prints, and that text can misrepresent what the tool actually did, even when the tool's computation is correct. We saw this happen in a production RAG research system used by the Pilsudski Institute in New York, where tool output formatters misled an agent into giving wrong or incomplete information to users. Each tool did its job correctly, but its output omitted search limits, result caps, or identifier namespaces. We also recreated an unlabeled estimate caught in code review before release. We studied whether these formatters misled agents and verifiers and how much the repaired wording helps. We fed tool results to agents using two formatter versions: one with the key omissions and one with all missing details clearly stated. That difference alone changed what the agents claimed and what the verifiers accepted. Unsupported agent claims dropped substantially for three of the four failure types. In one test, verifiers went from accepting incorrect answers 90 out of 90 times to rejecting them 90 out of 90 times. A control showed the verifiers could catch the errors once they were given the missing facts and asked to judge correctness. We include the audit prompt we used with Codex and Claude Code in an exploratory demonstration, written with prior knowledge of our own system's defects. When pointed at an old version of our own system, it rediscovered the defects that were still live and surfaced twelve more we had not catalogued. When pointed at OpenClaw and Hermes, two of the best-known open-source agentic systems, it found warped formatters in both. We opened PRs to fix both, and the OpenClaw fix has already been merged. Practitioners can run the same prompt on their own systems today.

top_articles.title: PaperFormalizer: Author-in-the-Loop Autoformalization of Research Papers in Lean
top_articles.title_original: PaperFormalizer: Author-in-the-Loop Autoformalization of Research Papers in Lean
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.31810v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Even a carefully proofread paper can leave small gaps in its proofs or its stated assumptions. We introduce PaperFormalizer, a Lean-based agentic pipeline that helps authors find and close such gaps in their own papers and turn each paper into a Lean-verified version. Starting from the LaTeX source, PaperFormalizer transcribes the paper into a dependency graph of statements, audits each statement in natural language for faithfulness, ambiguity and correctness, and then formalizes and proves the statements in Lean against Mathlib, optional domain libraries and the author's personal toolkit. Only the author knows what a statement is meant to say and how a formalization gap in a result is best fixed. The pipeline therefore stops and asks the author whenever a statement admits more than one reading, presents every repair, in natural language and TeX symbols, as a proposal that the author can accept, decline or redirect, and leaves to the author every decision that could potentially change what the paper claims. The output is an annotated and revised version of the paper, a report of the changes, and Lean code in which each declaration is linked to the statement it formalizes. The author's toolkit grows as more papers are formalized, and authors can share their verified papers so that researchers who build on them can reuse their Lean code. By making verified papers practical to produce, PaperFormalizer aims to make research that rests on mathematical proofs more robust. PaperFormalizer runs inside a coding agent (Claude Code or Codex) and is available at https://github.com/Jiyuan-Tan/PaperFormalizer. Papers with Lean code shared by users are available at https://paperformalizer.org.

top_articles.title: Don't Forget What You Just Learned: Self-Directed Repair Turns Agent Mistakes Into Lasting Lessons
top_articles.title_original: Don't Forget What You Just Learned: Self-Directed Repair Turns Agent Mistakes Into Lasting Lessons
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.31846v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Intelligent agents should learn from their mistakes so that experience leads to continuous improvement. Yet today's agents recover from a mistake only temporarily: in-context reflections are easily forgotten across sessions and compete for limited context, while full-parameter fine-tuning is expensive and can interfere with existing capabilities. We introduce Self-Direction, a mechanism for agents to learn from mistakes that combines the benefits of temporary in-context retries and policy updates. When an agent fails a task, it reflects on its own trajectory in order to extract a lesson and immediately distills it into a lightweight low-rank adapter. By keeping the original weights frozen, Self-Direction prevents adapter training from overwriting base-model parameters while training additional parameters equivalent to ~0.02% of the base model's parameter count for each adapter. The agent then saves these adapters in a persistent library of lessons, automatically routing them to solve related problems later. Experiments with agents based on open-weight models from the Qwen family across open-ended research (GAIA), tool-use workflows (Claw-Eval), and terminal tasks (Terminal-Bench 2.1) show that our method improves overall success rates by 8.9 to 17.0 percentage points and performs competitively with frontier systems. We find that Self-Direction reduces repeated mistakes across future encounters of a task, nearly doubling the reliability of an agent's corrections. Learned lessons also transfer: a handful of adapters generalize to dozens of new tasks without additional training. Ultimately, this self-directed repair transforms everyday mistakes into lasting lessons.

top_articles.title_original: 中国信通院：6 月国内词元日均消耗量约 500 万亿，是 2025 年 12 月的近 4 倍
top_articles.summary: IT之家 10 月 24 日消息，据中国信通院，随着大模型技术的迅速迭代，词元（Token）服务成为从技术走向应用的关键点，我国日均词元调用量持续攀升，2026 年 6 月， 国内词元日均消耗量约 500 万亿 ，是 2025 年 12 月的近 4 倍。产业中越来越多的 MaaS（Model as a Service，模型即服务）平台厂商通过公有云 API 方式供给大模型词元服务。然而用户对词元服务性能缺乏直观的判断依据，且面临选型困难等各类问题。 为有效衡量服务性能，中国信息通信研究院（简称“中国信通院”）人工智能研究所、人工智能大模型及软硬件评测工业和信息化部重点实验室和中国人工智能产业发展联盟，自 2025 年以来持续开展公有云大模型词元服务性能监测工作，为产业应用提供重要参考，现联合发布《大模型词元服务性能监测报告（2026 年）》。 报告基于 2026 年 1-8 月的监测数据，围绕各平台词元服务调用成功率、吞吐速度、首词时延、稳定性、价格、上下文窗口等维度开展分析，对比原厂大模型官方平台，以及 DeepSeek、Qwen、GLM、Kimi 四款开源模型在第三方平台上的性能差异，进一步分析影响词元服务性能的关键因素，总结产业核心观察，明确下一步工作计划，旨在为用户选型提供参考，并为产业界优化服务能力提供方向指引。 IT之家附报告核心观点： 1. 国内词元服务每秒吞吐量较 2025 年翻倍，仍低于国外 报告提出，8 月份国内各模型平均 TPS（每秒输出词元数）达到 78.23（个 / 秒），与 2025 年均值 38.25（个 / 秒）相比实现翻倍。但 8 月份国外典型模型的 TPS 均值为 112.82（个 / 秒），与 2025 年 12 月的 51.35（个 / 秒）相比，提升亦超过一倍，整体优于国内。 ▲ 所有大模型词元服务月均 TPS 2. 词元服务时延有所增加，国内外趋势一致 报告提出，今年以来，国内各模型的平均 TTFT（首词时延）呈现持续提升态势，8 月份均值达到 1.26 秒，相较于 2025 年平均值 0.78 秒明显增加。但同时 8 月份国外典型模型 TTFT 平均值达到 2.08 秒，相比 4 月份 1.04 秒亦明显增加。值得注意的是，TTFT 上升并非单纯的性能退化，而是伴随着模型参数量增加、上下文长度增加、调用量增加等多种因素同步产生的结果。 ▲ 所有大模型词元服务的月均 TTFT 3. 2026 年词元服务价格明显回升 报告提出，经历了过去两年价格战后，2026 年国内外模型服务价格明显上涨。国内 2025 下半年归一化均价为 6.8 元，而今年以来均价为 13.46 元，涨幅接近 1 倍。但国外价格仍高于国内，2026 年以来发布的典型模型平均归一价格约为 117.8 元。 ▲ 国内原厂大模型发布时归一化价格趋势图 4. 模型上下文长度不断向百万级长度扩展 报告提出，被监测的模型中，上下文长度达到 1M（1 百万词元）的模型占比 47.8%，200K 及以上的合计达 95.7%，相比 2025 年底的占比提高超过 76 个百分点，而低于 200K 的模型占比持续减少。 ▲ 国内原厂大模型发布时归一化价格趋势图 5. 开源模型词元服务性能提升显著，同一模型在不同平台性能波动较大 报告提出，5 月份更新了 4 款开源模型的新版本进行监测，结果显示 TPS 持续提升，TTFT 时延不断压缩。例如 8 月份 DeepSeek-V4-Pro 的 TPS 已达到 DeepSeek-V3.2 的 2 倍。时延方面，5 月份主要模型完成换代升级后，TTFT 普遍出现阶段性上升，随着推理优化措施落地，时延指标逐步回落至换代前水平。同时，4 款模型在不同平台上的 TPS、TTFT、调用成功率表现不一。部分第三方平台性能明显优于官方平台提供的模型服务，同一模型在不同平台间的 TPS 差距最大可接近一倍。各平台对相同模型的推理加速、优化策略、成本控制不同，是造成性能分化的主要原因。 ▲ 开源模型性能综合对比图

top_articles.title: SPECMEM: Accelerating Agentic Tool Calling via Live Memory Management
top_articles.title_original: SPECMEM: Accelerating Agentic Tool Calling via Live Memory Management
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.31840v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool-calling agents are mostly optimized for accuracy; in deployment, however, their growing cost is latency: every tool call is decoded autoregressively. Speculative decoding accelerates this without changing the output, and retrieved past calls make strong drafts under real use, where each user's behavior tends to repeat. Yet existing systems keep no cross-session memory, or build the draft store once and never update it. We propose SpecMem, a tool-call memory kept alive and managed throughout deployment: verified calls are written back online into bounded per-user stores with LRU eviction, and a side-effect gate defers irreversible calls until verification confirms. On multi-session, multi-user query streams served by three open-weight models, a frozen store steadily loses acceptance while SpecMem holds it: a 27% gap in mean accepted tokens (+11% to +34% across benchmarks, tracking how much novel work arrives after the store is built) and up to 1.74x wall-clock speedup. Ablations attribute the gain almost entirely to keeping the store live; local per-user scoping adds no acceptance but closes a measured cross-user leakage channel, and gating on declared side effects, rather than on retrieval confidence, is what eliminates irreversible mistakes.

top_articles.title: Spectral Smoothing and Spiking Perturbations Reconfigure Capability Profiles and Selective Task Performance in Large Language Models
top_articles.title_original: Spectral Smoothing and Spiking Perturbations Reconfigure Capability Profiles and Selective Task Performance in Large Language Models
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.30676v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Singular-value spectra encode important structure in transformer feed-forward projections, yet their causal role in downstream behavior remains underexplored. We study post-hoc spectral smoothing and spiking interventions on the up_proj and down_proj matrices. Positive perturbation stretches deviations from the geometric mean, making large singular values larger and small ones smaller (spiking), and vice versa. The intervention preserves singular vectors and the geometric mean of the singular values. Across five open Llama and Qwen instruction models, we evaluate the perturbed systems on capability-labeled subtasks, standard and chain-of-thought reasoning benchmarks, judge-scored truthfulness, hallucination, and safety tasks, and TRAIT personality probes. To interpret score shifts, we fit responses in a three-dimensional capability basis consisting of factual knowledge, language understanding, and deductive reasoning. The induced changes suggest structured rather than purely random sensitivity: large positive perturbations more reliably suppress language and deductive responses, moderate negative perturbations can sometimes improve factual or task-local performance on the evaluated grids, and sensitivity varies strongly by model family, benchmark module, and underlying layerwise spectral inequality. These results position spectral perturbation as a lightweight intervention for probing how capabilities are organized and traded off in large language models.

top_articles.title: Explore Separately, Adopt Selectively: Execution-Guided Tool Use over Large Tool Libraries
top_articles.title_original: Explore Separately, Adopt Selectively: Execution-Guided Tool Use over Large Tool Libraries
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.22688v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model agents must discover relevant tools from large libraries, e.g., thousands of tools, as new needs arise during task execution. When several candidates could satisfy the same need, execution may be required to identify the relevant one. Investigating candidates in a shared trajectory can leave alternatives unexplored or allow failed attempts to influence subsequent reasoning. To address this, we present BRIA (BRanch-Inspect-Adopt), a simple yet effective agent that temporarily isolates candidate investigations in separate branches. Each branch retrieves and executes tools to investigate its candidate; a task agent inspects the resulting execution evidence and adopts only useful results into its continuing trajectory. BRIA retrieves additional tools as new capability needs arise during task execution. We evaluate BRIA on PlanBench-XL and MCP-Atlas using a shared pool of 1897 tools, three language models, and static and adaptive retrieval baselines. Across all settings, BRIA matches or exceeds the strongest retrieval baseline. On MCP-Atlas, it achieves an average claim score of 89.77, compared with 75.40 for MCP-Zero, a gain of 14.37 percentage points. BRIA also lies on the Pareto frontier for task performance and input-token cost.

top_articles.title: Exploration via Activation-Space Steering for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
top_articles.title_original: Exploration via Activation-Space Steering for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.27012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains a language model by sampling responses, scoring them with an automatic verifier, and updating the policy from the resulting rewards. The policy therefore receives direct learning signals only from trajectories that appear in its rollouts. Yet repeated sampling from the same policy can concentrate on similar reasoning paths, leaving useful alternatives unexplored under a fixed rollout budget. We introduce Activation-Space Exploration (ASE), an online method for diversifying training rollouts. By clustering activation differences between correct and incorrect responses to the same problem, ASE builds a structured bank of latent exploration vectors. Different vectors are then applied to subsequent rollouts to explore alternative reasoning paths. On Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base trained on DAPO-Math-17k, ASE improves average Mean@8 across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks over GRPO by 4.87 and 1.87 percentage points, respectively, under the same rollout budget.

top_articles.title: ReAPO: Retry-Aware Policy Optimization for Efficient Exploration in LLM Reasoning
top_articles.title_original: ReAPO: Retry-Aware Policy Optimization for Efficient Exploration in LLM Reasoning
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.28770v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: RLVR improves language-model reasoning, but commonly relies on independent stochastic rollouts for exploration, which can repeatedly sample similar failed strategies. Prior work has seen success with approaches that guide exploration by introducing dependence into the sampling process by including incorrect solutions in the context for subsequent attempts. Still, these methods introduce the additional question of how to assign credit to each attempt. We propose to view the credit assignment through the lens of Stochastic Shortest Paths, a framework in classical reinforcement learning that seeks to minimize the expected cumulative cost to reach a terminal state (in our case, a verified successful response). We show that, under suitable simplifying assumptions, this perspective naturally leads to a simple modification to GRPO, which we call Retry-Aware Policy Optimization (ReAPO). ReAPO allocates additional generation to failed trajectories, allowing successful retries to be reinforced without rewarding preceding failures, and assigns credit in a theoretically principled way to each attempt. Across Qwen3 and OLMo-2 models from 0.6B to 4B and eight mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks, ReAPO improves first-attempt performance over GRPO as well as natural recent baseline algorithms, while additional ablations demonstrate the utility of both serial sampling and ReAPO's credit assignment. On Qwen3-0.6B, ReAPO also outperforms GRPO with twice the group size or twice the training steps, reaching their peak accuracy with 39% and 31% fewer generated tokens, respectively. Taken together, our results suggest that ReAPO is a simple yet effective approach for improving LM reasoning performance through improved exploration and retry-aware credit assignment.

top_articles.title: High-dimensional layer-state trajectories reveal the internal dynamics of transformer inference
top_articles.title_original: High-dimensional layer-state trajectories reveal the internal dynamics of transformer inference
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.26866v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mechanistic studies of large language models localize function in parameters, attention heads or neurons, but those parts do not specify how one inference unfolds. We treat the ordered layer-state trajectory as the empirical process and test whether layer order defines a measurable computation. Across representative Qwen, Llama and Gemma checkpoints, realized order produced paths 1.60--2.24 times as aligned with their endpoint chord as endpoint-preserving shuffles. The order effect transferred to a lexical task, but was stronger in three random initializations of the same Qwen architecture, identifying an architecture-compatible scaffold rather than a training-specific law. Direct hidden states provided stronger mechanism coordinates than vocabulary readbacks, and a task-defined coordinate made candidate competition computable. After additive interventions failed, local transition actuators selectively controlled internal trajectories across checkpoints. A confidence gate then drove 17 of 87 held-out Qwen closure trajectories across the full-vocabulary top-1 candidate boundary while leaving all 203 non-closure top-1 outputs unchanged. Safety-matched action reassignment performed similarly, locating the gain in selective gating and the bounded actuator family rather than fine-grained dose assignment. Layer order exposes an observable, computable and behaviourally consequential process of transformer inference without establishing a complete theory of LLM dynamics or control of answer correctness.

top_articles.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
top_articles.title_original: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
top_articles.summary: Redesigning source control at Anthropic Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart ( code here ) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026: This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity. "Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. ( Update : Anthropic credit Google's Piper and Meta's Sapling as "prior art" - it looks like the core concept of "derived data" was heavily inspired by Mononoke , the server component of Sapling.) They had some pretty extreme requirements: The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day. The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months. When asked on Hacker News about the lack of offline support, Scion engineer Nick G replied : Since Claude is by far the heaviest user of Scion and is necessarily online, this just wasn't important to do. As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). This note from the article reflected my own experience with that: Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns. top_articles.title: Who Verifies the Tools? How Warped Formatters Mislead Agents and Their Verifiers
top_articles.title_original: Who Verifies the Tools? How Warped Formatters Mislead Agents and Their Verifiers
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.32110v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agents and verifiers often rely on the text a tool prints, and that text can misrepresent what the tool actually did, even when the tool's computation is correct. We saw this happen in a production RAG research system used by the Pilsudski Institute in New York, where tool output formatters misled an agent into giving wrong or incomplete information to users. Each tool did its job correctly, but its output omitted search limits, result caps, or identifier namespaces. We also recreated an unlabeled estimate caught in code review before release. We studied whether these formatters misled agents and verifiers and how much the repaired wording helps. We fed tool results to agents using two formatter versions: one with the key omissions and one with all missing details clearly stated. That difference alone changed what the agents claimed and what the verifiers accepted. Unsupported agent claims dropped substantially for three of the four failure types. In one test, verifiers went from accepting incorrect answers 90 out of 90 times to rejecting them 90 out of 90 times. A control showed the verifiers could catch the errors once they were given the missing facts and asked to judge correctness. We include the audit prompt we used with Codex and Claude Code in an exploratory demonstration, written with prior knowledge of our own system's defects. When pointed at an old version of our own system, it rediscovered the defects that were still live and surfaced twelve more we had not catalogued. When pointed at OpenClaw and Hermes, two of the best-known open-source agentic systems, it found warped formatters in both. We opened PRs to fix both, and the OpenClaw fix has already been merged. Practitioners can run the same prompt on their own systems today.

top_articles.title: PaperFormalizer: Author-in-the-Loop Autoformalization of Research Papers in Lean
top_articles.title_original: PaperFormalizer: Author-in-the-Loop Autoformalization of Research Papers in Lean
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.31810v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Even a carefully proofread paper can leave small gaps in its proofs or its stated assumptions. We introduce PaperFormalizer, a Lean-based agentic pipeline that helps authors find and close such gaps in their own papers and turn each paper into a Lean-verified version. Starting from the LaTeX source, PaperFormalizer transcribes the paper into a dependency graph of statements, audits each statement in natural language for faithfulness, ambiguity and correctness, and then formalizes and proves the statements in Lean against Mathlib, optional domain libraries and the author's personal toolkit. Only the author knows what a statement is meant to say and how a formalization gap in a result is best fixed. The pipeline therefore stops and asks the author whenever a statement admits more than one reading, presents every repair, in natural language and TeX symbols, as a proposal that the author can accept, decline or redirect, and leaves to the author every decision that could potentially change what the paper claims. The output is an annotated and revised version of the paper, a report of the changes, and Lean code in which each declaration is linked to the statement it formalizes. The author's toolkit grows as more papers are formalized, and authors can share their verified papers so that researchers who build on them can reuse their Lean code. By making verified papers practical to produce, PaperFormalizer aims to make research that rests on mathematical proofs more robust. PaperFormalizer runs inside a coding agent (Claude Code or Codex) and is available at https://github.com/Jiyuan-Tan/PaperFormalizer. Papers with Lean code shared by users are available at https://paperformalizer.org.

top_articles.title: Don't Forget What You Just Learned: Self-Directed Repair Turns Agent Mistakes Into Lasting Lessons
top_articles.title_original: Don't Forget What You Just Learned: Self-Directed Repair Turns Agent Mistakes Into Lasting Lessons
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.31846v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Intelligent agents should learn from their mistakes so that experience leads to continuous improvement. Yet today's agents recover from a mistake only temporarily: in-context reflections are easily forgotten across sessions and compete for limited context, while full-parameter fine-tuning is expensive and can interfere with existing capabilities. We introduce Self-Direction, a mechanism for agents to learn from mistakes that combines the benefits of temporary in-context retries and policy updates. When an agent fails a task, it reflects on its own trajectory in order to extract a lesson and immediately distills it into a lightweight low-rank adapter. By keeping the original weights frozen, Self-Direction prevents adapter training from overwriting base-model parameters while training additional parameters equivalent to ~0.02% of the base model's parameter count for each adapter. The agent then saves these adapters in a persistent library of lessons, automatically routing them to solve related problems later. Experiments with agents based on open-weight models from the Qwen family across open-ended research (GAIA), tool-use workflows (Claw-Eval), and terminal tasks (Terminal-Bench 2.1) show that our method improves overall success rates by 8.9 to 17.0 percentage points and performs competitively with frontier systems. We find that Self-Direction reduces repeated mistakes across future encounters of a task, nearly doubling the reliability of an agent's corrections. Learned lessons also transfer: a handful of adapters generalize to dozens of new tasks without additional training. Ultimately, this self-directed repair transforms everyday mistakes into lasting lessons.

top_articles.title_original: 中国信通院：6 月国内词元日均消耗量约 500 万亿，是 2025 年 12 月的近 4 倍
top_articles.summary: IT之家 10 月 24 日消息，据中国信通院，随着大模型技术的迅速迭代，词元（Token）服务成为从技术走向应用的关键点，我国日均词元调用量持续攀升，2026 年 6 月， 国内词元日均消耗量约 500 万亿 ，是 2025 年 12 月的近 4 倍。产业中越来越多的 MaaS（Model as a Service，模型即服务）平台厂商通过公有云 API 方式供给大模型词元服务。然而用户对词元服务性能缺乏直观的判断依据，且面临选型困难等各类问题。 为有效衡量服务性能，中国信息通信研究院（简称“中国信通院”）人工智能研究所、人工智能大模型及软硬件评测工业和信息化部重点实验室和中国人工智能产业发展联盟，自 2025 年以来持续开展公有云大模型词元服务性能监测工作，为产业应用提供重要参考，现联合发布《大模型词元服务性能监测报告（2026 年）》。 报告基于 2026 年 1-8 月的监测数据，围绕各平台词元服务调用成功率、吞吐速度、首词时延、稳定性、价格、上下文窗口等维度开展分析，对比原厂大模型官方平台，以及 DeepSeek、Qwen、GLM、Kimi 四款开源模型在第三方平台上的性能差异，进一步分析影响词元服务性能的关键因素，总结产业核心观察，明确下一步工作计划，旨在为用户选型提供参考，并为产业界优化服务能力提供方向指引。 IT之家附报告核心观点： 1. 国内词元服务每秒吞吐量较 2025 年翻倍，仍低于国外 报告提出，8 月份国内各模型平均 TPS（每秒输出词元数）达到 78.23（个 / 秒），与 2025 年均值 38.25（个 / 秒）相比实现翻倍。但 8 月份国外典型模型的 TPS 均值为 112.82（个 / 秒），与 2025 年 12 月的 51.35（个 / 秒）相比，提升亦超过一倍，整体优于国内。 ▲ 所有大模型词元服务月均 TPS 2. 词元服务时延有所增加，国内外趋势一致 报告提出，今年以来，国内各模型的平均 TTFT（首词时延）呈现持续提升态势，8 月份均值达到 1.26 秒，相较于 2025 年平均值 0.78 秒明显增加。但同时 8 月份国外典型模型 TTFT 平均值达到 2.08 秒，相比 4 月份 1.04 秒亦明显增加。值得注意的是，TTFT 上升并非单纯的性能退化，而是伴随着模型参数量增加、上下文长度增加、调用量增加等多种因素同步产生的结果。 ▲ 所有大模型词元服务的月均 TTFT 3. 2026 年词元服务价格明显回升 报告提出，经历了过去两年价格战后，2026 年国内外模型服务价格明显上涨。国内 2025 下半年归一化均价为 6.8 元，而今年以来均价为 13.46 元，涨幅接近 1 倍。但国外价格仍高于国内，2026 年以来发布的典型模型平均归一价格约为 117.8 元。 ▲ 国内原厂大模型发布时归一化价格趋势图 4. 模型上下文长度不断向百万级长度扩展 报告提出，被监测的模型中，上下文长度达到 1M（1 百万词元）的模型占比 47.8%，200K 及以上的合计达 95.7%，相比 2025 年底的占比提高超过 76 个百分点，而低于 200K 的模型占比持续减少。 ▲ 国内原厂大模型发布时归一化价格趋势图 5. 开源模型词元服务性能提升显著，同一模型在不同平台性能波动较大 报告提出，5 月份更新了 4 款开源模型的新版本进行监测，结果显示 TPS 持续提升，TTFT 时延不断压缩。例如 8 月份 DeepSeek-V4-Pro 的 TPS 已达到 DeepSeek-V3.2 的 2 倍。时延方面，5 月份主要模型完成换代升级后，TTFT 普遍出现阶段性上升，随着推理优化措施落地，时延指标逐步回落至换代前水平。同时，4 款模型在不同平台上的 TPS、TTFT、调用成功率表现不一。部分第三方平台性能明显优于官方平台提供的模型服务，同一模型在不同平台间的 TPS 差距最大可接近一倍。各平台对相同模型的推理加速、优化策略、成本控制不同，是造成性能分化的主要原因。 ▲ 开源模型性能综合对比图

top_articles.title: SPECMEM: Accelerating Agentic Tool Calling via Live Memory Management
top_articles.title_original: SPECMEM: Accelerating Agentic Tool Calling via Live Memory Management
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.31840v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool-calling agents are mostly optimized for accuracy; in deployment, however, their growing cost is latency: every tool call is decoded autoregressively. Speculative decoding accelerates this without changing the output, and retrieved past calls make strong drafts under real use, where each user's behavior tends to repeat. Yet existing systems keep no cross-session memory, or build the draft store once and never update it. We propose SpecMem, a tool-call memory kept alive and managed throughout deployment: verified calls are written back online into bounded per-user stores with LRU eviction, and a side-effect gate defers irreversible calls until verification confirms. On multi-session, multi-user query streams served by three open-weight models, a frozen store steadily loses acceptance while SpecMem holds it: a 27% gap in mean accepted tokens (+11% to +34% across benchmarks, tracking how much novel work arrives after the store is built) and up to 1.74x wall-clock speedup. Ablations attribute the gain almost entirely to keeping the store live; local per-user scoping adds no acceptance but closes a measured cross-user leakage channel, and gating on declared side effects, rather than on retrieval confidence, is what eliminates irreversible mistakes.

top_articles.title: Spectral Smoothing and Spiking Perturbations Reconfigure Capability Profiles and Selective Task Performance in Large Language Models
top_articles.title_original: Spectral Smoothing and Spiking Perturbations Reconfigure Capability Profiles and Selective Task Performance in Large Language Models
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.30676v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Singular-value spectra encode important structure in transformer feed-forward projections, yet their causal role in downstream behavior remains underexplored. We study post-hoc spectral smoothing and spiking interventions on the up_proj and down_proj matrices. Positive perturbation stretches deviations from the geometric mean, making large singular values larger and small ones smaller (spiking), and vice versa. The intervention preserves singular vectors and the geometric mean of the singular values. Across five open Llama and Qwen instruction models, we evaluate the perturbed systems on capability-labeled subtasks, standard and chain-of-thought reasoning benchmarks, judge-scored truthfulness, hallucination, and safety tasks, and TRAIT personality probes. To interpret score shifts, we fit responses in a three-dimensional capability basis consisting of factual knowledge, language understanding, and deductive reasoning. The induced changes suggest structured rather than purely random sensitivity: large positive perturbations more reliably suppress language and deductive responses, moderate negative perturbations can sometimes improve factual or task-local performance on the evaluated grids, and sensitivity varies strongly by model family, benchmark module, and underlying layerwise spectral inequality. These results position spectral perturbation as a lightweight intervention for probing how capabilities are organized and traded off in large language models.

top_articles.title: Explore Separately, Adopt Selectively: Execution-Guided Tool Use over Large Tool Libraries
top_articles.title_original: Explore Separately, Adopt Selectively: Execution-Guided Tool Use over Large Tool Libraries
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.22688v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model agents must discover relevant tools from large libraries, e.g., thousands of tools, as new needs arise during task execution. When several candidates could satisfy the same need, execution may be required to identify the relevant one. Investigating candidates in a shared trajectory can leave alternatives unexplored or allow failed attempts to influence subsequent reasoning. To address this, we present BRIA (BRanch-Inspect-Adopt), a simple yet effective agent that temporarily isolates candidate investigations in separate branches. Each branch retrieves and executes tools to investigate its candidate; a task agent inspects the resulting execution evidence and adopts only useful results into its continuing trajectory. BRIA retrieves additional tools as new capability needs arise during task execution. We evaluate BRIA on PlanBench-XL and MCP-Atlas using a shared pool of 1897 tools, three language models, and static and adaptive retrieval baselines. Across all settings, BRIA matches or exceeds the strongest retrieval baseline. On MCP-Atlas, it achieves an average claim score of 89.77, compared with 75.40 for MCP-Zero, a gain of 14.37 percentage points. BRIA also lies on the Pareto frontier for task performance and input-token cost.

top_articles.title: Exploration via Activation-Space Steering for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
top_articles.title_original: Exploration via Activation-Space Steering for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.27012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains a language model by sampling responses, scoring them with an automatic verifier, and updating the policy from the resulting rewards. The policy therefore receives direct learning signals only from trajectories that appear in its rollouts. Yet repeated sampling from the same policy can concentrate on similar reasoning paths, leaving useful alternatives unexplored under a fixed rollout budget. We introduce Activation-Space Exploration (ASE), an online method for diversifying training rollouts. By clustering activation differences between correct and incorrect responses to the same problem, ASE builds a structured bank of latent exploration vectors. Different vectors are then applied to subsequent rollouts to explore alternative reasoning paths. On Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base trained on DAPO-Math-17k, ASE improves average Mean@8 across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks over GRPO by 4.87 and 1.87 percentage points, respectively, under the same rollout budget.

top_articles.title: ReAPO: Retry-Aware Policy Optimization for Efficient Exploration in LLM Reasoning
top_articles.title_original: ReAPO: Retry-Aware Policy Optimization for Efficient Exploration in LLM Reasoning
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.28770v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: RLVR improves language-model reasoning, but commonly relies on independent stochastic rollouts for exploration, which can repeatedly sample similar failed strategies. Prior work has seen success with approaches that guide exploration by introducing dependence into the sampling process by including incorrect solutions in the context for subsequent attempts. Still, these methods introduce the additional question of how to assign credit to each attempt. We propose to view the credit assignment through the lens of Stochastic Shortest Paths, a framework in classical reinforcement learning that seeks to minimize the expected cumulative cost to reach a terminal state (in our case, a verified successful response). We show that, under suitable simplifying assumptions, this perspective naturally leads to a simple modification to GRPO, which we call Retry-Aware Policy Optimization (ReAPO). ReAPO allocates additional generation to failed trajectories, allowing successful retries to be reinforced without rewarding preceding failures, and assigns credit in a theoretically principled way to each attempt. Across Qwen3 and OLMo-2 models from 0.6B to 4B and eight mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks, ReAPO improves first-attempt performance over GRPO as well as natural recent baseline algorithms, while additional ablations demonstrate the utility of both serial sampling and ReAPO's credit assignment. On Qwen3-0.6B, ReAPO also outperforms GRPO with twice the group size or twice the training steps, reaching their peak accuracy with 39% and 31% fewer generated tokens, respectively. Taken together, our results suggest that ReAPO is a simple yet effective approach for improving LM reasoning performance through improved exploration and retry-aware credit assignment.

top_articles.title: High-dimensional layer-state trajectories reveal the internal dynamics of transformer inference
top_articles.title_original: High-dimensional layer-state trajectories reveal the internal dynamics of transformer inference
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.26866v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mechanistic studies of large language models localize function in parameters, attention heads or neurons, but those parts do not specify how one inference unfolds. We treat the ordered layer-state trajectory as the empirical process and test whether layer order defines a measurable computation. Across representative Qwen, Llama and Gemma checkpoints, realized order produced paths 1.60--2.24 times as aligned with their endpoint chord as endpoint-preserving shuffles. The order effect transferred to a lexical task, but was stronger in three random initializations of the same Qwen architecture, identifying an architecture-compatible scaffold rather than a training-specific law. Direct hidden states provided stronger mechanism coordinates than vocabulary readbacks, and a task-defined coordinate made candidate competition computable. After additive interventions failed, local transition actuators selectively controlled internal trajectories across checkpoints. A confidence gate then drove 17 of 87 held-out Qwen closure trajectories across the full-vocabulary top-1 candidate boundary while leaving all 203 non-closure top-1 outputs unchanged. Safety-matched action reassignment performed similarly, locating the gain in selective gating and the bounded actuator family rather than fine-grained dose assignment. Layer order exposes an observable, computable and behaviourally consequential process of transformer inference without establishing a complete theory of LLM dynamics or control of answer correctness.
